questions.prompt: If do_work() throws an exception after t is launched below, what happens when stack unwinding destroys t?
options: ~std::thread() automatically calls t.join() before propagating the exception
~std::thread() automatically detaches t so it runs in the background
~std::thread() calls std::terminate() because t.joinable() is still true
Compilation fails because std::thread requires a try/catch block
questions.explanation: Because t was neither joined nor detached before unwinding reached ~std::thread(), t.joinable() remains true. Under [thread.thread.destr], destroying a joinable std::thread immediately calls std::terminate(), unlike C++20 std::jthread, which requests stop and joins automatically.

questions.prompt: What bug exists in the transfer function below?
options: std::scoped_lock(m1, m2); creates an unnamed temporary that locks and immediately unlocks at the semicolon, leaving the critical section unprotected
std::scoped_lock deadlocks when passed two mutexes
std::scoped_lock only accepts one mutex in C++23
The function leaks both mutexes when returning
questions.explanation: Because no variable name is given, std::scoped_lock(m1, m2); constructs a temporary object whose lifetime ends at the semicolon, unlocking m1 and m2 right before the critical section executes. Writing std::scoped_lock lk(m1, m2); binds a named guard to the scope.

questions.prompt: Look closely at the member declaration order inside Pipeline. Why is ~Pipeline() unsafe when Pipeline goes out of scope?
options: std::jthread cannot capture this in its constructor lambda
std::scoped_lock cannot be constructed inside a while loop
~jthread() does not call request_stop() unless stop_source is passed manually
Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so mtx_ is destroyed BEFORE ~jthread() requests stop and joins worker_
questions.explanation: Class data members are always destroyed in reverse order of declaration ([class.dtor]). Because worker_ is declared first, mtx_ and active_ are destroyed first while worker_ is still running its loop—invoking undefined behavior. Declaring std::jthread worker_; last guarantees it stops and joins before mtx_ and active_ die.

questions.prompt: Thread A needs to signal Thread B that a buffer is ready, so Thread B can proceed and unblock. Which synchronization primitive is legal when Thread A unlocks/signals and Thread B acquires?
options: Locking a std::mutex on Thread B and calling m.unlock() from Thread A
Calling sem.release() on Thread A and sem.acquire() on Thread B with std::binary_semaphore sem{0}
Destroying a std::lock_guard created on Thread A from Thread B
Using std::shared_lock on Thread A and unlocking it from Thread B
questions.explanation: std::mutex has strict thread ownership: unlocking a mutex from a thread that does not own the lock is undefined behavior ([thread.mutex.requirements.mutex]). By contrast, std::counting_semaphore and std::binary_semaphore have no thread ownership—any thread may call release() while another calls acquire().

questions.prompt: Why does std::condition_variable_any::wait(lk, st, pred) still check pred() inside a loop, even with a std::stop_token?
options: Only std::condition_variable suffers from spurious wakeups; condition_variable_any never wakes spuriously
A stop_token disables mutex locking inside condition_variable_any
Condition variable waits may experience spurious wakeups ([thread.condition.condvarany]), so the overload loops until either pred() returns true or st.stop_requested() becomes true
wait(lk, st, pred) throws std::system_error when st.stop_requested() is true
questions.explanation: Under [thread.condition.condvarany], wait(lock, stoken, pred) repeatedly waits while !stoken.stop_requested() and !pred(), returning pred() once either the predicate holds or stop was requested. This handles both spurious wakeups and stop requests delivered before or during the wait.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately captures the C++ standard rules for std::barrier's CompletionFunction and std::call_once's callable if exceptions occur?
options: std::barrier catches and ignores exceptions thrown by CompletionFunction, while std::call_once marks the once_flag permanently failed on exception
Both std::barrier and std::call_once call std::terminate() if their callables throw
Neither std::barrier nor std::call_once constrains exceptions on its callable
std::barrier mandates std::is_nothrow_invocable_v<CompletionFunction&> (noexcept), whereas an exception from std::call_once leaves the once_flag uncompleted so another thread retries
questions.explanation: Under [thread.barrier], std::barrier<CompletionFunction> requires is_nothrow_invocable_v<CompletionFunction&> to be true (a non-noexcept completion callable is ill-formed). Under [thread.once.callonce], an invocation of std::call_once that exits via an exception is classified as an exceptional execution rather than returning, allowing a subsequent waiting invocation to try again.
